arXiv:1305.1173v1 [math.CA] 06 May 2013

Total positivity of a Cauchy kernel

Thomas Simon Address: Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, Université Lille 1, Cité Scientifique, F-59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq Cedex. Email: simon@math.univ-lille1.fr
Abstract.

We study the total positivity of the kernel 1/(x2+2​cos⁡(π​α)​x​y+y2).1/(x^{2}+2\cos(\pi\alpha)xy+y^{2}). The case of infinite order is characterized by an application of Schoenberg’s theorem. We then give necessary conditions for the cases of any given finite order with the help of Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. Sufficient conditions for the finite order cases are also obtained, thanks to Propp’s formula for the Izergin-Korepin determinant. As a by-product, we give a partial answer to a question of Karlin on positive stable semi-groups.

Key words and phrases: 
Alternating sign matrix - Cauchy kernel - Chebyshev polynomial - Izergin-Korepin determinant - Positive stable semi-group - Total positivity
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
15A15, 15B48, 33C45, 60E07

1. Introduction

Let II be some real interval and KK some real kernel defined on I×II\times I. The kernel KK is called totally positive of order nn (TPn{\rm TP}_{n}) if

det[K⁡(xi,yj)]1≤i,j≤m≥ 0\det\left[K(x_{i},y_{j})\right]_{1\leq i,j\leq m}\;\geq\;0

for every m∈{1,…,n},x1<…<xmm\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\,x_{1}<\ldots<x_{m} and y1<…<ym.y_{1}<\ldots<y_{m}. If these inequalities hold for all nn one says that KK is TP∞{\rm TP}_{\infty}. The kernel KK is called sign-regular of order nn (SRn{\rm SR}_{n}) if there exists {εm}1≤m≤n∈{−1,1}\{\varepsilon_{m}\}_{1\leq m\leq n}\in\{-1,1\} such that

εm​det[K⁡(xi,yj)]1≤i,j≤m≥ 0\varepsilon_{m}\det\left[K(x_{i},y_{j})\right]_{1\leq i,j\leq m}\;\geq\;0

for every m∈{1,…,n},x1<…<xmm\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\,x_{1}<\ldots<x_{m} and y1<…<ym.y_{1}<\ldots<y_{m}. If these inequalities hold for all nn one says that KK is SR∞{\rm SR}_{\infty}. The above four properties are called strict, with corresponding notations STP and SSR, when all involved inequalities are strict. We refer to [7] for the classic account on this field and its various connections with analysis, especially Descartes’ rule of signs. We also mention the recent monograph [11] for a more linear algebraic point of view and updated references.

A function f:ℝ→ℝ+f:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+} is called Pólya frequency of order n≤∞n\leq\infty (PFn{\rm PF}_{n}) if the kernel K⁡(x,y)=f⁡(x−y)K(x,y)=f(x-y) is TPn{\rm TP}_{n} on ℝ×ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}}. When this kernel is STPn,{\rm STP}_{n}, we will use the notation f∈SPFn.f\in{\rm SPF}_{n}. Probability densities belonging to the class PF∞{\rm PF}_{\infty} have been characterized by Schoenberg - see e.g. Theorem 7.3.2 (i) p. 345 in [7] - through the meromorphic extension of their Laplace transform, whose reciprocal is an entire function having the following Hadamard factorization:

(1) 1𝔼⁡[es​X]=e−γ​s2+δ​s​∏n=0∞(1+an​s)​e−an​s\frac{1}{{\mathbb{E}}[e^{sX}]}\;=\;e^{-\gamma s^{2}+\delta s}\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}(1+a_{n}s)e^{-a_{n}s}

with XX the associated random variable, γ≥0,δ∈ℝ,\gamma\geq 0,\,\delta\in{\mathbb{R}}, and ∑an2<∞.\sum a_{n}^{2}<\infty. The classical example is the Gaussian density. PF2{\rm PF}_{2} functions are easily characterized by the log-concavity on their support - see Theorems 4.1.8 and 4.1.9 in [7]. But except for the cases n=2n=2 or n=∞n=\infty there is no handy criterion for testing the PFn{\rm PF}_{n} character of a given function resp. the TPn{\rm TP}_{n} character of a given kernel, and such questions might be difficult. In this paper we consider the kernel

Kα​(x,y)=1x2+2​cos⁡(π​α)​x​y+y2K_{\alpha}(x,y)\;=\;\frac{1}{x^{2}+2\cos(\pi\alpha)xy+y^{2}}

over (0,+∞)×(0,+∞),(0,+\infty)\times(0,+\infty), with α∈[0,1).\alpha\in[0,1). Because of its proximity with the standard Cauchy density we may call KαK_{\alpha} a Cauchy kernel, eventhough the denomination Poisson kernel would also be justified. Occurrences of the kernel KαK_{\alpha} in the literature are many and varied. We show the following

Theorem​​ .

(a) One has

Kα∈STP∞⇔Kα∈SR∞⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…,0}.K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm STP}_{\infty}\,\Leftrightarrow\,K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm SR}_{\infty}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots,0\}.

(b) For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

Kα∈TPn⇔Kα∈SRn⇒α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}​or​α<1/n.K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm TP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm SR}_{n}\,\Rightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;\alpha<1/n.

(c) For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has α≤1/n∧1/(n2−n−6)+⇒Kα∈STPn.\alpha\leq 1/n\wedge 1/(n^{2}-n-6)_{+}\,\Rightarrow\,K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm STP}_{n}.

The well-known fact that K0K_{0} and K1/2K_{1/2} are STP∞{\rm STP}_{\infty} is a direct consequence of explicit classical formulæ  for the involved determinants, due respectively to Cauchy and Borchardt - see e.g. (2.7) and (3.9) in [8] - and which will be recalled thereafter. The characterization obtained in Part (a) follows without difficulty from Schoenberg’s theorem and Gauss’ multiplication formula, and will be given in Section 2. The more involved proofs of Part (b) and Part (c) rely both on an analysis of the derivative determinant

Δαn=detn[∂i+j−2Kα∂xi−1​∂yj−1]\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}\;=\;{\det}_{n}\left[\frac{\partial^{i+j-2}K_{\alpha}}{\partial x^{i-1}\partial y^{j-1}}\right]

where, here and throughout, we set detn{\det}_{n} for the determinant of a matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by (i,j)∈{1,…,n}2.(i,j)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}. To obtain Part (b) we establish a closed expression for Δαn​(1,0+)\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(1,0+) in terms of Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, an expression which is negative whenever α∉{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}\alpha\not\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\} or α>1/n.\alpha>1/n. The computations are performed in Section 3, in four manners involving respectively Wronskians, Schur functions, rectangular matrices and alternating sign matrices. The observation that these four very different approaches all lead to the same formula was interesting to the author. On the other hand only the last approach, which is based on Propp’s formula for the Izergin-Korepin determinant, seems successful to get the more difficult Part (c). This latter result is partial because our upper condition on α\alpha is probably not optimal. We raise the

Conjecture​​ .

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

(2) α<1/n⇒Kα∈STPn.\alpha<1/n\;\Rightarrow\;K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm STP}_{n}.

This would show that the inclusion in Part (b) is actually an equivalence, which is true for n=2,3n=2,3 by Part (c) of the theorem because then n≥(n2−n−6)+.n\geq(n^{2}-n-6)_{+}. In Section 5 we show (2) for n=4,5n=4,5, and we also give some heuristics reasons supporting the validity of this inclusion for all nn. The latter seems however to require wild computations. In Section 5, we state three other conjectures of combinatorial nature whose fulfilment would entail (2). The most natural one is a criterion for the positivity of the generating function

fn,k​(z)=∑A∈𝒜nμ⁡(A)=kzν⁡(A)​z¯ν⁡(AQ)f_{n,k}(z)\;=\;\sum_{\tiny\begin{array}[]{c}A\!\in\!{\mathcal{A}}_{n}\\ \mu(A)\!=\!k\end{array}}\!\!\!\!z^{\nu(A)}{\bar{z}}^{\nu(A^{Q})}

evaluated at a certain complex number zz, where 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is the set of alternating sign matrices of size nn, AQA^{Q} is the anticlockwise quarter-turn rotation of A,A, μ⁡(A)\mu(A) is the number of negative entries and ν⁡(A)\nu(A) the inversion number (see the precise notations below). Whereas we can show this criterion for k=0k=0 or k=μmaxk=\mu_{\rm max} (see below Propositions 3 and 4), unfortunately we cannot do so for all kk since there is no sufficiently explicit general formula for fn,kf_{n,k}. Let us stress that the single evaluation of fn,k​(1)=♯⁡{A∈𝒜n,μ⁡(A)=k}f_{n,k}(1)=\sharp\{A\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n},\,\mu(A)=k\} is a difficult open problem, solved only for certain values of kk - see [10] and the references therein.

The present paper was initially motivated by a question of S. Karlin - see Section 6 below for its precise statement - on the total positivity in space-time of the positive stable semi-group (t,x)↦pα​(t,x)(t,x)\mapsto p_{\alpha}(t,x) on (0,+∞)×(0,+∞),(0,+\infty)\times(0,+\infty), which we recall to be defined by the Laplace transform

(3) ∫0∞pα​(t,x)​e−λ​x​𝑑x=e−t​λα,λ≥0.\int_{0}^{\infty}p_{\alpha}(t,x)e^{-\lambda x}\,dx\;=\;e^{-t\lambda^{\alpha}},\qquad\lambda\geq 0.

As a simple consequence of Part (b), in Section 6 we show the

Corollary​​ .

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, one has

pα∈SRn⇒α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n}​or​α<1/n.p_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm SR}_{n}\,\Rightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n\}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;\alpha<1/n.

The inclusion α≤1/n⇒pα∈TPn\alpha\leq 1/n\,\Rightarrow\,p_{\alpha}\in{\rm TP}_{n} was proved in [12] for n=2n=2 and we believe that it is true in general. This would give a complete answer to Karlin’s question and also entail the above conjecture - see Section 6 for an explanation. This will be the matter of further research.

2. Proof of part (a)

This easy part of the theorem is a consequence of the following Proposition 1 and Corollary 1.

Proposition 1.

One has

Kα∈STP∞⇔Kα∈TP∞⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…,0}.K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm STP}_{\infty}\;\Leftrightarrow\;K_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm TP}_{\infty}\;\Leftrightarrow\;\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots,0\}.

where the right-hand side follows from the residue theorem and is meant as a limit for α=0.\alpha=0. If α∉{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…,0},\alpha\notin\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots,0\}, the function

s↦α​sin⁡(π​s)sin⁡(π​α​s)s\;\mapsto\;\frac{\alpha\sin(\pi s)}{\sin(\pi\alpha s)}

has a pole at 1/α1/\alpha so that gα∉PF∞g_{\alpha}\not\in{\rm PF}_{\infty} by the aforementioned Theorem 7.3.2 (i) in [7]. If α=1/n\alpha=1/n for some n≥2,n\geq 2, writing

(4) sin⁡(π​s)n​sin⁡(π​s/n)=Γ⁡(1−s)​Γ​(1+s)Γ⁡(1−s/n)​Γ​(1+s/n)\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{n\sin(\pi s/n)}\;=\;\frac{\Gamma(1-s)\Gamma(1+s)}{\Gamma(1-s/n)\Gamma(1+s/n)}

and applying Gauss’ multiplication formula and Weierstrass formula for the Gamma function - see e.g. 1.2(11) p.4 and 1.1(3) p.1 in [5] - shows that this function is of the type (1), in other words that gα∈PF∞.g_{\alpha}\in{\rm PF}_{\infty}. If α=0,\alpha=0, the same conclusion holds true thanks to the Eulerian formula

sin⁡(π​s)π​s=∏n≥1(1−s2n2)⋅\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi s}\;=\;\prod_{n\geq 1}\left(1-\frac{s^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)\cdot

detn[1xi2+yj2]=∏1≤i<j≤n(yj2−yi2)​(xj2−xi2)∏1≤i,j≤n(xi2+yj2){\det}_{n}\left[\frac{1}{x_{i}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}}\right]\;=\;\frac{\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(y_{j}^{2}-y_{i}^{2})(x_{j}^{2}-x_{i}^{2})}{\prod_{1\leq i,j\leq n}(x_{i}^{2}+y_{j}^{2})}

Remark 1.

(a) The above argument based on the composition formula yields the STP∞{\rm STP}_{\infty} character of all kernels (a​x+b​y+c)−d(ax+by+c)^{-d} for a,b,d>0a,b,d>0 and c≥0c\geq 0 (this is the main result of [4] - see Theorem 3.1 therein), in writing

Kα​(x,y)=∫0∞e−x2​u​Lα​(u,y)​𝑑u.K_{\alpha}(x,y)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}u}\,L_{\alpha}(u,y)du.

Kα∈TPn⇔Lα∈RRnK_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm TP}_{n}\Leftrightarrow L_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm RR}_{n}

for all n.n.

We give four different proofs of (8), each corresponding to a specific approach to evaluate the derivative determinant Δαn​(x,y)\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y) in closed form. The first two proofs involve classical tools, respectively Wronskians and Schur functions. The last two proofs rely on more elaborate and recent results on the Izergin-Korepin determinant, using combinatorial formulæ  due respectively to Lascoux and Propp. The latter formula, involving alternating sign matrices, will be also used to obtain Part (c).

3.1. Wronskians

We fix α∈[0,1),\alpha\in[0,1), set cα=cos⁡(π​α)c_{\alpha}=\cos(\pi\alpha) and sα=sin⁡(π​α).s_{\alpha}=\sin(\pi\alpha). We use the notations

For every n≥0,n\geq 0, one has

The formula is obviously true for n=0,1.n=0,1. By induction, it suffices to show that

Remark 3.

It does not seem that (10) and standard Wronskian transformations can provide any information which is enough explicit to characterize the everywhere positivity of (x,y)↦Δαn​(x,y).(x,y)\mapsto\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y). The latter is crucial for (2) - see Section 4 below.

3.2. Schur functions

This second approach relies on the following well-known expression for the generating function of Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind:

∑k≥0Uk+1α​zk=Kα​(1,−z),|z|<1.\sum_{k\geq 0}U^{\alpha}_{k+1}z^{k}\;=\;K_{\alpha}(1,-z),\qquad|z|<1.

This entails

Dαn​(X,Y)=1∏j=1nxj2​detn[∑k≥0Uk+1α​(yi​zj)k]{\rm D}_{\alpha}^{n}(X,Y)\;=\;\frac{1}{{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}^{2}}}\;{\det}_{n}\left[\sum_{k\geq 0}U^{\alpha}_{k+1}(y_{i}z_{j})^{k}\right]

with the above notation for XX and Y,Y, having written zj=−xj−1z_{j}=-x_{j}^{-1} and assuming, here and throughout, |yi​zj|<1|y_{i}z_{j}|<1 for all i,j=1,…,n.i,j=1,\ldots,n. The determinant on the right-hand side, denoted by Fαn​(X,Y),F_{\alpha}^{n}(X,Y), can be further evaluated by multilinear expansion:

Fαn​(X,Y)=∑k1​…​kn=0∞detn[zjki]​(∏l=1nUkl+1α​ylkl).F_{\alpha}^{n}(X,Y)\;=\;\sum_{k_{1}\ldots k_{n}=0}^{\infty}{\det}_{n}\left[z_{j}^{k_{i}}\right]\left(\prod_{l=1}^{n}U^{\alpha}_{k_{l}+1}y_{l}^{k_{l}}\right).

Notice that in the multiple sum, all indices kik_{i} can be chosen distinct since otherwise the summand is zero. Setting 𝒮n{\mathcal{S}}_{n} for the symmetric group of size nn and

UKα=∏l=1nUkl+1αU_{{\rm K}}^{\alpha}\;=\;\prod_{l=1}^{n}U^{\alpha}_{k_{l}+1}

for any n−n-tuple K=(k1,…,kn),{\rm K}=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}), one obtains

Fαn​(X,Y)\displaystyle F_{\alpha}^{n}(X,Y) =\displaystyle= ∑k1>⋯>kn≥0UKα​(∑σ∈𝒮ndetn[zjkσ⁡(i)]​(∏l=1nylkσ⁡(l)))\displaystyle\sum_{k_{1}>\cdots>k_{n}\geq 0}U_{{\rm K}}^{\alpha}\left(\sum_{\sigma\in{\mathcal{S}}_{n}}{\det}_{n}\left[z_{j}^{k_{\sigma(i)}}\right]\left(\prod_{l=1}^{n}y_{l}^{k_{\sigma(l)}}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑k1>⋯>kn≥0UKα​detn[zjki]​detn[yjki],\displaystyle\sum_{k_{1}>\cdots>k_{n}\geq 0}U_{{\rm K}}^{\alpha}\;{\det}_{n}\left[z_{j}^{k_{i}}\right]{\det}_{n}\left[y_{j}^{k_{i}}\right],

where in the second equality we used twice Leibniz’s formula. The above can now be rewritten in terms of Schur functions and Vandermonde determinants. Setting ki=n−i+λi,k_{i}=n-i+\lambda_{i}, one has

Fαn​(X,Y)\displaystyle F_{\alpha}^{n}(X,Y) =\displaystyle= ∑λ1≥⋯≥λn≥0UKα​detn[zjn−i+λi]​detn[yjn−i+λi]=VY​VZ​∑λUKα​sλ​(Y)​sλ​(Z)\displaystyle\sum_{\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{n}\geq 0}U_{{\rm K}}^{\alpha}\;{\det}_{n}\left[z_{j}^{n-i+\lambda_{i}}\right]{\det}_{n}\left[y_{j}^{n-i+\lambda_{i}}\right]\;=\;V_{Y}V_{Z}\;\sum_{\lambda}U_{{\rm K}}^{\alpha}\;s_{\lambda}(Y)s_{\lambda}(Z)

where in the second equality the sum is meant on all partitions of size nn and we use the standard notation for Schur functions, displayed e.g. in Chapter 4 p.124 of [3]. Putting everything together and differentiating with (7) yield after some simplifications

Δαn​(x,y)=sf​(n−1)2xn⁡(n+1)/2​∑λ(∏i=1nUn−i+λi+1α)​sλ​(1,…,1)2​(−y​x−1)|λ|\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y)\;=\;\frac{{\rm sf}(n-1)^{2}}{x^{n(n+1)/2}}\sum_{\lambda}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}U^{\alpha}_{n-i+\lambda_{i}+1}\right)s_{\lambda}(1,\ldots,1)^{2}(-yx^{-1})^{|\lambda|}

for all 0<y<x,0<y<x, with the notation |λ|=λ1+⋯+λn.|\lambda|=\lambda_{1}+\cdots+\lambda_{n}. By the change of variable μi=λn+1−i,\mu_{i}=\lambda_{n+1-i}, the classical formula

sλ​(1,…,1)=∏1≤i<j≤n(λi−λj+j−i)sf⁡(n−1)s_{\lambda}(1,\ldots,1)\;=\;\frac{\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}+j-i)}{{\rm sf}(n-1)}

which can be recovered from the Jacobi-Trudi identity - see e.g. Proposition 4.2 in [3] - and a standard binomial determinant evaluation, entails finally

(14) Δαn​(x,y)=1xn⁡(n+1)/2​∑k=0∞(−y​x−1)k​∑μ1≤⋯≤μnμ1+⋯+μn=k(∏i=1nUi+μiα)​∏1≤i<j≤n(μj−μi+j−i)2.\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y)\;=\;\frac{1}{x^{n(n+1)/2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-yx^{-1})^{k}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{{\tiny\begin{array}[]{c}\mu_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\mu_{n}\\ \mu_{1}+\cdots+\mu_{n}=k\end{array}}}\!\!\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\;U^{\alpha}_{i+\mu_{i}}\right)\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(\mu_{j}-\mu_{i}+j-i)^{2}.

Remark 4.

Because of the alternate signs, the above expression (14) does not seem very helpful either to study the everywhere positivity of Δαn​(x,y).\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y).

3.3. Rectangular matrices

This third approach hinges upon a certain closed expression for the determinant

Dq​(X,Y)=detn[1(xi+yj)​(q​xi+yj)].{\rm D}_{q}(X,Y)\;=\;{\det}_{n}\left[\frac{1}{(x_{i}+y_{j})(qx_{i}+y_{j})}\right].

The latter is called the Izergin-Korepin determinant in the literature, and appears in the context of the six-vertex model - see Chapter 7 in [3]. We use its evaluation in terms of rectangular matrices separating the variables, which is due to Lascoux - see Theorem qq in [9]. It is given by

Dq​(X,Y)=VX​VYPq​(X,Y)​detn[HX×EYq]{\rm D}_{q}(X,Y)\;=\;\frac{V_{X}V_{Y}}{{\rm P}_{q}(X,Y)}\,{\det}_{n}\left[H_{X}\times E^{q}_{Y}\right]

where Pq​(X,Y)=∏1≤i,j≤n(xi+yj)​(q​xi+yj),{\rm P}_{q}(X,Y)\;=\;\prod_{1\leq i,j\leq n}(x_{i}+y_{j})(qx_{i}+y_{j}), and

HX=[hk−i​(X)]1≤i≤n,1≤k≤2​n−1,EYq=[qk−j+1−qj−1q−1​en−k+j−1​(Y)]1≤k≤2​n−1,1≤j≤nH_{X}\;=\;\left[h_{k-i}(X)\right]_{1\leq i\leq n,1\leq k\leq 2n-1},\qquad E^{q}_{Y}\;=\;\left[\frac{q^{k-j+1}-q^{j-1}}{q-1}\,e_{n-k+j-1}(Y)\right]_{1\leq k\leq 2n-1,1\leq j\leq n}

are two rectangular matrices involving the complete resp. elementary symmetric functions, which we recall to be defined through the generating functions

(15) ∑k≥0hk​(X)​tk=∏r=1n(1−xr​t)−1and∑k≥0ek​(Y)​tk=∏r=1n(1+yr​t).\sum_{k\geq 0}h_{k}(X)t^{k}\;=\;\prod_{r=1}^{n}(1-x_{r}t)^{-1}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\sum_{k\geq 0}e_{k}(Y)t^{k}\;=\;\prod_{r=1}^{n}(1+y_{r}t).

EYy=[Cnn−k+j−1​q(k−1)/2​Uk+2−2​jα​yn−k+j−1]1≤k≤2​n−1,1≤j≤n,E_{Y_{y}}\;=\;\left[C^{n-k+j-1}_{n}q^{(k-1)/2}U_{k+2-2j}^{\alpha}y^{n-k+j-1}\right]_{1\leq k\leq 2n-1,1\leq j\leq n},

5. Open questions

In this section we give some heuristic reasons supporting the validity of the inclusion

(25) α<1/n⇒Δαn​(x,y)>0for all x,y>0\alpha<1/n\;\Rightarrow\;\Delta_{\alpha}^{n}(x,y)>0\quad\mbox{for all $x,y>0$}

which, by the ETP criterion and an immediate induction, is enough to show (2). First, we formulate a conjecture on the positivity of certain generating functions of ASM matrices which would entail (25), and we test it on the values n=3,4,5.n=3,4,5. Second, we discuss more thoroughly Lascoux’s factorization and settle two problems on the positivity on certain minors of rectangular matrices involving Chebyshev polynomials, whose solution would again entail (25).

5.1. Alternating sign matrices

By (21), the positivity of Δαn\Delta_{\alpha}^{n} amounts to that of

∑A∈𝒜nPαμ⁡(A)​Qα2​ν​(A)​Q¯α2​ν​(AQ),\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n}}P_{\alpha}^{\mu(A)}Q_{\alpha}^{2\nu(A)}{\bar{Q}}_{\alpha}^{2\nu(A^{Q})},

with the notations of Section 4. The above sum can be expressed with the bivariate generating function

which is itself given as a certain functional determinant - see Formula (57) p. 21 in [1]. Unfortunately the latter determinant is in general very difficult to evaluate, except in certain particular cases. Its value at x=y=1,x=y=1, counting the cardinal of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, was the matter of a whole story which is told in the book [3]. As in the proof of Part (c) let us now write

For every n≥2n\geq 2 and every k=0,…,μn,k=0,\ldots,\mu_{n}, one has Fn,kα>0F^{\alpha}_{n,k}>0 whenever α≤1/n.\alpha\leq 1/n.

5.2. Rectangular matrices

In this paragraph we study in more details the minors Aσ​(1){\rm A}_{\sigma}(1) and Bσα​(1),{\rm B}_{\sigma}^{\alpha}(1), with the notations of Section 3.3. Indeed, formulæ  (16), (17) and (18) show that the positivity of Δαn\Delta_{\alpha}^{n} is ensured by that of Aσ​(1){\rm A}_{\sigma}(1) and Bσα​(1).{\rm B}_{\sigma}^{\alpha}(1). The analysis for Aσ​(1){\rm A}_{\sigma}(1) is easy.

and the last sum clearly vanishes. This persymmetry entails Bσ​(1)=Bσ~​(1).{\rm B}_{\sigma}(1)={\rm B}_{\tilde{\sigma}}(1). We now state a natural conjecture which would entail (25).

Conjecture 2.

For every n≥2,n\geq 2, all coefficients Bσ​(1){\rm B}_{\sigma}(1) are positive whenever α<1/n.\alpha<1/n.

The difficulty to prove this conjecture comes from the rectangular shape of the matrices {Bα,n},\{B_{\alpha,n}\}, which makes it seemingly impossible to use any kind of induction argument. Let us finally display the five first elements of the sequence {Bα,n},\{B_{\alpha,n}\}, whose common shape reminds that of Trinidad and Tobago’s national flag (the red background being the zeroes, the crucial white diagonal stripes Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, and the black central parallelogram positive linear combinations thereof) and displays some spatial unimodality around the middle.

and

Bα,5=(5​U1α10​U2α10​U3α5​U4αU5α⋯0010​U2α10​U3α+50​U1α5​U4α+50​U2αU5α+25​U3α⋯00010​U3α5​U4α+50​U2αU5α+25​U3α+100​U1α⋯00005​U4αU5α+25​U3α⋯00000U5α⋯5​U1α).B_{\alpha,5}=\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}5U^{\alpha}_{1}&10U^{\alpha}_{2}&10U^{\alpha}_{3}&5U^{\alpha}_{4}&U^{\alpha}_{5}&\cdots&0\\ 0&10U^{\alpha}_{2}&10U^{\alpha}_{3}+50U^{\alpha}_{1}&5U^{\alpha}_{4}+50U^{\alpha}_{2}&U^{\alpha}_{5}+25U^{\alpha}_{3}&\cdots&0\\ 0&0&10U^{\alpha}_{3}&5U^{\alpha}_{4}+50U^{\alpha}_{2}&U^{\alpha}_{5}+25U^{\alpha}_{3}+100U^{\alpha}_{1}&\cdots&0\\ 0&0&0&5U^{\alpha}_{4}&U^{\alpha}_{5}+25U^{\alpha}_{3}&\cdots&0\\ 0&0&0&0&U^{\alpha}_{5}&\cdots&5U^{\alpha}_{1}\end{array}\!\!\right).

Using some elementary trigonometry, for these first five values of nn we could check that Bα,nB_{\alpha,n} is TP (viz. all its minors are non-negative) if α<1/n\alpha<1/n The following is hence natural

Conjecture 3.

For every n≥1,n\geq 1, the matrix Bα,nB_{\alpha,n} is TP whenever α<1/n.\alpha<1/n.

This conjecture is stronger than Conjecture 2 since it involves all minors. Notice that several criteria have appeared in recent years to prove the total positivity of a given matrix without checking every minor. See all the results mentioned in Section 2.5 of [11] and also Theorem 2.16 therein for a criterion only on 2×22\times 2 minors, interestingly also related to the zeroes of Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. Unfortunately, none of this criteria seems particularly helpful in our situation.

6. Proof of the corollary

Setting fα​(x)=pα​(1,x),f_{\alpha}(x)=p_{\alpha}(1,x), we see from (3) that pα(t,x)=t−1/αfα(xt−1/α),p_{\alpha}(t,x)=t^{-1/\alpha}f_{\alpha}(xt^{-1/\alpha}), so that by Theorem 1.2.1. p.18 in [7] the kernel pα​(t,x)p_{\alpha}(t,x) has the same sign-regularity over (0,+∞)×(0,+∞)(0,+\infty)\times(0,+\infty) than the kernel fα​(ex−y)f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y}) over ℝ×ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}}. In Paragraph 7.12.E p.390 of [7] it is shown that

fα​(ex−y)∈STP∞⇔fα​(ex−y)∈TP∞⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…}f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y})\,\in\,{\rm STP}_{\infty}\;\Leftrightarrow\;f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y})\,\in\,{\rm TP}_{\infty}\;\Leftrightarrow\;\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots\}

and the question is raised whether fα​(ex−y)f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y}) should be TP of some finite order when α\alpha is not the reciprocal of an integer. In [12], we obtained the equivalence fα​(ex−y)∈TP2⇔α≤1/2.f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y})\,\in\,{\rm TP}_{2}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\leq 1/2.

Let us now prove the Corollary. We need to show that if α\alpha is not the reciprocal of an integer and α<1/n,\alpha<1/n, then fα​(ex−y)∉SRn.f_{\alpha}(e^{x-y})\not\in{\rm SR}_{n}. If this were true, then the kernels fα​(ey−x)f_{\alpha}(e^{y-x}) and

ex−y​∫ℝfα​(ex−u)​fα​(eu−y)​𝑑ue^{x-y}\,\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{\alpha}(e^{x-u})f_{\alpha}(e^{u-y})\,du

would also be SRn{\rm SR}_{n} by Theorem 1.2.1. and Lemma 3.1.1. in [7]. However, a well-known fractional moment identification - see (3.1) in [12] and the references therein - shows that the latter kernel equals gα​(x−y)g_{\alpha}(x-y) with the notations of Section 2. Hence, we get a contradiction to Part (b) of the theorem.

□\Box

We finish this paper with a natural conjecture on the total positivity of the positive stable kernel pα,p_{\alpha}, which reformulates Karlin’s question in a more precise manner. By Lemma 3.1.1. in [7] and the same argument as in the proof of the corollary, this would also show the conjecture stated in the introduction. But we believe that this last conjecture is harder because the kernel pαp_{\alpha} is not explicit in general.

Conjecture 4.

For every n≥2n\geq 2 one has

pα∈STPn⇔pα∈SRn⇔α∈{1/2,1/3,…,1/n,…}​or​α<1/n.p_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm STP}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,p_{\alpha}\,\in{\rm SR}_{n}\,\Leftrightarrow\,\alpha\in\{1/2,1/3,\ldots,1/n,\ldots\}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;\alpha<1/n.
